facts.statehood_note: Louisiana entered the Union as a slave state, nine years after the United States bought the Louisiana Purchase lands from France in 1803.
facts.nickname: The Pelican State (also called Sportsman's Paradise)
facts.name_origin: The French explorer Robert de La Salle named it for Louis XIV, King of France, when he claimed the lower Mississippi valley in 1682.

government.chambers: Louisiana Senate (39 senators) and Louisiana House of Representatives (105 representatives); members of both chambers serve 4-year terms, with a limit of three terms in a row in each chamber
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; a person who has served more than one and one-half terms in two consecutive terms cannot be elected to the next term). Other statewide executive officials also serve 4-year terms.
government.courts: Louisiana Supreme Court (a chief justice and six associate justices, 7 in all), elected from at least six supreme court districts for 10-year terms; four justices must agree to decide a case.
government.local: 64 parishes instead of counties. The name comes from church districts (parishes) set up under Spanish rule in 1769, which the new state kept for its local regions.
government.constitution: Louisiana's current constitution is the Constitution of 1974. Its Article I begins by saying government comes from the people and exists to protect their rights.
government.kid_line: "No person shall be denied the equal protection of the laws." (Article I, Section 3)

long_ago.about: Between about 1700 and 1100 BCE, a society of hunter-fisher-gatherers built five mounds and six curved ridges across more than 400 acres, moving about 53 million cubic feet of soil. They brought in tons of stone from as far as 1,000 miles away.

The Chitimacha homeland stretched across coastal Louisiana from the Atchafalaya Basin to the New Orleans area. They traded game, plants, deerskins, bear oil, and salt, and Chitimacha women are famous for split-rivercane baskets.

The Caddo lived in permanent villages in the Red River valley of northwestern Louisiana, farming maize, beans, squash, and pumpkins and making pottery, cane baskets, and shell work. In 1835 they were forced to give up their lands east of the Sabine River.

The Ishak, a name that means roughly "the people," lived from Vermilion Bay in Louisiana to Galveston Bay in Texas and hunted bison. The name "Atakapa" came from a Choctaw word that colonists later used to justify mistreating them.

The Tunica were skilled traders, especially in salt, and the French depended on them for salt, rice, cattle, and horses. They settled near Marksville in the 1780s, and the Tunica, Biloxi, Ofo, and Avoyel later joined together as one tribe.

today.about: Based at Charenton in St. Mary Parish, it was the first tribe in Louisiana to gain federal recognition, in 1916.
Based at Elton in Allen Parish, it won state recognition in 1972 and federal recognition about fourteen months later.
Based at Marksville, it gained federal recognition in 1981, has about 1,500 enrolled members, and keeps the returned Tunica Treasure in its cultural center.
Based at Trout in LaSalle Parish, it organized a tribal government in 1973 and gained federal recognition in 1995.

first_peoples.today_note: Louisiana has four federally recognized tribes and eleven state-recognized tribes: the Adai Caddo Indians of Louisiana, Bayou Lafourche Band of Biloxi-Chitimachas, Choctaw-Apache Tribe of Ebarb, Clifton Choctaw Tribe of Louisiana, Four Winds Cherokee, Grand Caillou/Dulac Band of Biloxi Chitimacha Choctaw, Jean Charles Choctaw Nation, Louisiana Band of Choctaw Indian, Natchitoches Tribe of Louisiana, United Houma Nation, and Pointe-au-Chien Indian Tribe. The Caddo Nation, forced out in 1835, is based today in Binger, Oklahoma.
sites: Poverty Point World Heritage Site (northeast Louisiana): earthworks built about 1700 to 1100 BCE
Tunica-Biloxi cultural center (Marksville): displays the Tunica Treasure, returned to the tribe in 1989
Atchafalaya Basin: part of the Chitimacha homeland

history.event: Hunter-fisher-gatherers build and use the giant earthworks at Poverty Point.
Hernando de Soto's Spanish expedition reaches the Mississippi River and meets ancestors of the Tunica in the province of Quizquiz, in present-day northwestern Mississippi.
La Salle claims the lower Mississippi valley for France and names it Louisiana for King Louis XIV, though Indigenous nations already lived there.

The French found Fort St. Jean Baptiste near Natchitoches (1714), the first permanent settlement, and Bienville founds New Orleans (1718). In 1718 a twelve-year war with the French ends by treaty, forcing the Chitimacha to leave their lower Mississippi lands.
France issues the Code Noir, laws controlling enslaved Africans in the colony. In 1729 the Natchez attack the French at Fort Rosalie, and some enslaved people help them.
France gives Louisiana to Spain. Acadians arrive in 1765, and Spanish church parishes are set up in 1769.

Spanish authorities capture and execute Juan San Malo, a leader of maroons (people who escaped slavery). In 1795 a planned uprising at Pointe Coupée is betrayed, and sugar growing begins in south Louisiana.
The United States buys the Louisiana Purchase from France for $15 million.

Charles Deslondes leads 150 to 500 enslaved people on a march toward New Orleans in the German Coast uprising, the largest slave revolt in U.S. history. Militia and federal troops crush it, and close to 100 rebels die.
Louisiana becomes the 18th state, a slave state.
The Caddo are forced to give up their homeland east of the Sabine River to the United States.

Louisiana secedes on January 26, 1861. Union forces take New Orleans in April 1862, and Black Union soldiers of the Native Guards attack Confederate forts at Port Hudson on May 27, 1863. The Civil War ends slavery in Louisiana.

During Reconstruction, P. B. S. Pinchback becomes the first African American governor of any U.S. state. White supremacist violence follows, including the Colfax massacre (1873) and the White League's attack in New Orleans at the Battle of Liberty Place (1874).
Federal troops withdraw from Louisiana, ending Reconstruction.

trailblazers.name: Juan San Malo
trailblazers.text: He was a leader of maroons, people who escaped slavery and lived on their own. When Spanish Governor Esteban Miró cracked down on maroon communities in 1783 and 1784, San Malo was captured and executed in June 1784.

trailblazers.name: Charles Deslondes
trailblazers.text: He led the German Coast uprising of January 1811, when 150 to 500 enslaved people marched in military formation, with drums and flags, toward New Orleans to win their freedom. It was the largest revolt of enslaved people in U.S. history.

trailblazers.name: Henriette Delille
trailblazers.text: Born free in New Orleans, she founded the Sisters of the Holy Family in 1842 with Juliette Gaudin and Josephine Charles to serve the poor, enslaved people, and free people of color, even though laws restricted free people of color. The congregation continues today, its sisters later founded schools, orphanages, and nursing homes, and in 2010 the Pope named her Venerable.

trailblazers.name: André Cailloux
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved, he gained his freedom around 1846 and became a captain in the 1st Louisiana Native Guard, a Black Union regiment. He was killed leading his company at Port Hudson on May 27, 1863, and thousands attended his funeral in New Orleans, which inspired more Black men to join the Union army.

trailblazers.name: P. B. S. Pinchback
trailblazers.text: A captain in a Union Native Guards regiment, he became lieutenant governor in 1871 and served as governor for 36 days in 1872–1873, the first African American governor of any U.S. state. He later helped write the creation of Southern University into the 1879 state constitution.

trailblazers.name: Helen Gindrat
trailblazers.years: led the state Office of Indian Affairs in the early 1980s
trailblazers.text: A member of the Houma people, she was appointed executive director of the Louisiana Office of Indian Affairs, the state agency that works with Louisiana's tribes, in the early 1980s, before Clyde Jackson of the Jena Band of Choctaw Indians took the post in 1983.

landforms: Coastal marshes, swamps, and barrier islands
Atchafalaya Basin (largest river swamp in the U.S.)
Northern uplands with prairie, woodland, and longleaf pine
Driskill Mountain, the highest point (535 feet)
geography.regions: Louisiana has two main natural regions: the northern uplands of prairie, woodland, and longleaf pine, and the low alluvial and coastal lands of the south, with river swamps, marshes, and barrier islands built by the Mississippi River.

ecosystems.name: Atchafalaya river swamp
ecosystems.about: The largest river swamp in the United States covers more than 1.4 million acres, including about 885,000 acres of forested wetlands with cypress-tupelo swamps. More than 170 kinds of birds, 40 mammals, 40 reptiles, and 100 kinds of fish and shellfish live there, and Louisiana black bears live in its forests and farmland.

ecosystems.name: Coastal marshes and barrier islands
ecosystems.about: Louisiana holds 40 percent of the coastal wetlands in the lower 48 states, one of the world's most productive ecosystems. Marshes and barrier islands also protect towns like New Orleans from storms.

ecosystems.name: Gulf estuaries
ecosystems.about: Where rivers meet the Gulf, fish, shrimp, and crabs feed and grow, but nutrient-fed low-oxygen water along the coast can drive them away.

ecosystems.name: Northern uplands
ecosystems.about: North Louisiana's higher ground holds prairie, woodland, and longleaf pine forest, a different world from the swamps and marshes of the south.

science.weather: Louisiana has a humid subtropical climate and is very vulnerable to hurricanes; large storms hit the coast about every five years. Hurricane Katrina (August 29, 2005) broke levees and flooded more than 80 percent of New Orleans, and an August 2016 storm caused major flooding around Baton Rouge and Lafayette. The state also averages about 27 tornadoes and more than 60 thunderstorm days a year.
science.resources: Oil and natural gas, often trapped around underground salt domes, are major resources, along with seafood from the coast and Gulf.
science.highlight: Louisiana's disappearing coast: the state has 80 percent of U.S. coastal wetland losses, losing as much as 20 to 25 square miles of land a year, from sinking land, rising seas, storms, and human changes such as flood control and navigation channels. The Atchafalaya deltas are the only places along the Louisiana coast where land is growing.

g3_ss.title: Louisiana's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Baton Rouge, New Orleans, and the 64 parishes, learn why Louisiana has parishes, and learn what the Legislature, governor, and Supreme Court do.

g3_ss.title: Louisiana's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Visit Poverty Point and meet the Chitimacha, Coushatta, Tunica-Biloxi, Jena Band of Choctaw, and Houma, with a look at Chitimacha basketry.

g3_ss.title: Louisiana Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Meet Henriette Delille, André Cailloux, P. B. S. Pinchback, and Helen Gindrat.

g45_ss.title: Louisiana's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Study Poverty Point, the Caddo, Chitimacha, Ishak, and Tunica, and how Louisiana's tribes won recognition in the 1900s.

g45_ss.title: French and Spanish Louisiana
g45_ss.plan: Trace La Salle, New Orleans, the Chitimacha war, the Code Noir, the Acadians, Spanish parishes, maroons like Juan San Malo, and the growth of sugar and slavery.

g45_ss.title: Louisiana 1803–1877: Purchase, Resistance, War, and Reconstruction
g45_ss.plan: Examine the Louisiana Purchase, the 1811 German Coast uprising, statehood, Caddo land loss, the Native Guards at Port Hudson, the end of slavery, Pinchback, and the violent end of Reconstruction.

g3_sci.title: Swamp Life
g3_sci.plan: Explore the Atchafalaya swamp and its cypress trees, birds, alligators, and black bears.

g3_sci.title: Hurricane Safety
g3_sci.plan: Learn how hurricanes form over the warm Gulf and how families prepare and stay safe.

g3_sci.title: The Brown Pelican
g3_sci.plan: Study the state bird, how it dives for fish, and what it needs from a healthy coast.

g45_sci.title: The Disappearing Coast
g45_sci.plan: Investigate why Louisiana loses land each year and how river sediment builds new land at the Atchafalaya deltas.

g45_sci.title: The Mighty Mississippi Delta
g45_sci.plan: Learn how the Mississippi River built south Louisiana and how levees changed the flow of water and mud.

g45_sci.title: Mounds of Poverty Point
g45_sci.plan: Use math and science to estimate how much soil people moved to build Poverty Point and where their trade stones came from.
